strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem—evaluating the worst-case robustness of LLM watermarks—and provides a concrete, detector-free attack that substantially advances the state of the art in watermark removal. The empirical results (e.g., 98.5% ESR with 0.92 P-SP on 1500-token Unigram with Qwen2.5-3B) are striking and clearly surpass strong baselines such as SIRA and zero-shot GPT-4o.

The experimental evaluation is broad and thorough: five attacker scales, three victim models, ten watermarking schemes spanning logit-based and sampling-based families, three text lengths (250/500/1500 tokens), and four datasets. The distinction between removal rate (Rem.) and ESR (which requires semantic preservation, P-SP > 0.7) is a sensible evaluation design that exposes the semantic-collapse failure mode of SIRA.

Data efficiency and practicality are convincingly demonstrated: 100 short (500-token) samples suffice, performance plateaus beyond 100 samples (Table 5/11), training completes in 0.5–1.5 hours on four A100s, and the attack requires zero detector access. The mixed-key (Table 6/13) and cross-model OOD (Table 4/9/10) ablations provide credible evidence of generalization.

Reproducibility is comparatively good: watermark hyperparameters are given in full (Appendix C.1), the GRPO objective and reward definitions are specified (Appendix C.3), per-scheme weight configurations are tabulated (Table 7), and the sensitivity analysis (Figure 5) honestly reports hyperparameter fragility.

The findings on system prompts and reasoning/test-time scaling as underexplored adversarial levers (Figures 3, 4a) are useful and actionable for the watermarking-security community, even if individually not deeply novel.
weaknesses: Theory–method gap and oversold theory. The paper claims to "theoretically prove that optimizing the attack context and model parameters can substantially reduce this radius." In reality Theorem 1 is a standard Donsker–Varadhan/sub-Gaussian change-of-measure bound that certifies robustness (a lower bound on the radius), and the "reduction" claim reduces to the trivial monotonicity of an infimum over a larger set. The certified radius only "collapses to zero" when μ ≤ δ by the (x)_+^2 form, which is definitional rather than an insight into why the attack works.

The theory is never instantiated empirically. Neither r*(X), r_KL, nor ρ* is computed or measured for any watermarking scheme; the paper validates the attack, not the theory. Assumption 1 (sub-Gaussian detector scores) is stated but never verified, and the detector-score histograms in Figure 4(b) are not tested against it.

The RLCracker objective max_θ D_KL(Q||P_wm) − D_KL(Q||P_h) is asserted rather than derived from Theorem 1; the theorem concerns the detector score, not KL to P_wm/P_h. The practical reward uses a reference model conditioned on a paraphrasing prompt to approximate P_wm, which is a heuristic proxy with no clear theoretical grounding, and the paper itself admits the method is sensitive to w1/w2/w3.

The "generalizes across ten watermarking schemes" claim is weaker than stated: Table 7 shows that a dedicated RLCracker model (with scheme-specific weights) is trained per scheme. This is per-scheme fitting, not cross-scheme transfer; only the cross-key and cross-model results constitute genuine OOD generalization.

Baseline fairness. GPT-4o and DIPPER are zero-shot while RLCracker is fine-tuned on the target scheme, so the >90-point gaps (e.g., 98.5% vs. 6.75%) conflate training and capability. The dramatic GPT-4o numbers (P-SP as low as 0.58 on 1500-token Unigram) suggest the baselines may be under-prompted/under-tuned, and this weakens the headline comparison.

The attack is fundamentally a fine-tuned contrastive paraphraser; the marginal contribution of RL over a strong prompted/fine-tuned paraphraser is not isolated by an ablation (e.g., SFT-only or the same reward without GRPO). It is therefore hard to attribute the gains to the proposed RL formulation versus generic paraphrasing plus scheme-specific tuning.

Dual-use/ethics treatment is thin for a watermark-removal attack. The Broader Impact section is brief and offers little mitigation guidance or responsible-disclosure discussion, which is a notable omission given the offensive nature of the contribution.

strengths: Introduces a novel RL-based watermark removal attack (RLCracker) that achieves high evasion success rates with limited training data (100 samples) and no detector access.
Conducts extensive experiments across five attacker models and ten watermarking schemes, demonstrating broad effectiveness and generalization to out-of-distribution models and mixed-key scenarios.
Highlights the underappreciated impact of system prompts and reasoning capabilities on watermark robustness, offering useful insights for future evaluations.
Provides detailed hyperparameters and training configurations, which aids reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: The theoretical framework is poorly defined and not rigorously connected to the proposed attack. The notation for P_{s,c,θ} is ambiguous, and the main theorem is a standard application of sub-Gaussian concentration bounds, offering limited novel insight. The claimed theoretical contributions are overstated.

A crucial baseline is missing: a supervised fine-tuned model trained on the same 100 watermarked samples. Without this, it is unclear whether the RL component is necessary or if simple fine-tuning would achieve similar watermark removal, making the central claim unsupported.

The comparison to GPT-4o is unfair: GPT-4o is used zero-shot with a simple prompt, while RLCracker is fine-tuned on watermarked data. No attempt is made to optimize prompts or provide few-shot examples for GPT-4o.

No comparison to other state-of-the-art watermark removal attacks such as B4 (Huang et al., 2024) or WS (Jovanović et al., 2024), despite discussing them in related work. This makes it difficult to assess the relative significance of the contribution.
The KL divergence estimator used in the reward may be biased: it omits an importance sampling weight when sampling from the old policy, potentially leading to incorrect updates.
Ethical implications and potential defenses are not adequately discussed. The broader impact section is brief and does not propose mitigations, which is insufficient for a paper on attack methods.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or data is provided, and the exact training data and prompts used for RL training are not fully specified.
The abstract cherry-picks the best-case result (98.5% on 1500-token Unigram) while performance varies widely across schemes (e.g., 63.7% on Unigram for Qwen3-4B), which is misleading.
No confidence intervals or multiple runs are reported, making it difficult to assess statistical significance of the results.
The 'adaptive robustness radius' is never computed or evaluated; the paper only measures ESR. The theoretical metric remains disconnected from the empirical evaluation.

The claim that RLCracker 'enhances reasoning' is unsupported; the method does not explicitly incorporate reasoning steps, and the comparison to the 'Think' baseline does not isolate the reasoning component.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the worst-case robustness of LLM watermarking under adaptive adversaries, moving beyond average-case evaluations with fixed paraphrasers.

Proposes RLCracker, a novel reinforcement-learning-based watermark removal attack that requires only limited watermarked examples and no detector access. The method is empirically effective across many settings, e.g., 98.5% ESR on 1500-token Unigram-marked text with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct while maintaining a 0.92 P-SP score.

The paper introduces the adaptive robustness radius and a KL-divergence-based certificate. Although the theory is not fully operational, it provides a useful conceptual lens and connects watermark robustness to certified robustness and distributionally robust optimization.

Extensive experiments across five attacker model scales, three victim models, ten watermarking schemes, multiple token lengths (250/500/1500), and four datasets. The empirical breadth is impressive and the main trends are consistent.

Includes informative ablations and analyses: OOD cross-model generalization, training-set size, mixed-key training, prompt variation, reasoning depth, test-time scaling, and detection-score distribution alignment.

Highlights overlooked adversarial factors such as system prompts and reasoning/test-time scaling, showing that even relatively simple context enrichment can substantially degrade watermark robustness.

Reproducibility is partially supported: watermark hyperparameters are given via MarkLLM defaults, RLCracker hyperparameters are listed in Table 7, and training details/compute are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical framework is not tightly connected to the proposed attack. The instance-level adaptive robustness radius is relaxed to a distribution-level KL radius, but this relaxation does not directly preserve the original semantic guarantee. Theorem 1 is essentially a standard Donsker-Varadhan/sub-Gaussian bound, and the certificate rho* is never estimated or validated empirically.

The attack's core reward design relies on questionable approximations of the watermark distribution P_wm and human distribution P_h. P_wm is approximated by a reference model conditioned on the watermarked response, which is not the actual watermarking distribution; P_h is approximated by the same reference model conditioned on the question. The KL reward component is not ablated, so its necessity and correctness are not established.

Evaluation is potentially circular: P-SP is used both as the training semantic reward and as the criterion for successful watermark removal (P-SP > 0.7). High P-SP scores therefore partly reflect optimization against the metric rather than independent evidence of semantic fidelity. No human evaluation or alternative semantic metric is provided.

The claim of generalization across ten watermarking schemes is somewhat misleading. The appendix states that a dedicated RLCracker model is trained for each watermarking scheme, with scheme-specific weights in Table 7. Thus the method does not demonstrate a single model that generalizes to unseen schemes; it requires per-scheme training and tuning.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or suspicious. SIRA and DIPPER achieve near-zero ESR across many settings, often with very low P-SP scores (e.g., SIRA P-SP around 0.25-0.47), which suggests implementation or evaluation issues. GPT-4o is not given the same SysP/Think context enrichment as open models in the main table, making the comparison less informative.

The paper motivates RLCracker via Pass@k attacks but does not directly compare RLCracker to an oracle Pass@k upper bound in the main results. The claim that RL approaches Pass@k performance is therefore not fully substantiated.

No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported despite many close comparisons across tables. Some differences may be within noise, especially for smaller models and shorter token lengths.

The broader-impact and ethics discussion is superficial for an attack paper that releases an effective watermark-removal method. There is no discussion of dual-use risks, responsible disclosure, or mitigation strategies. A limitations section is also absent; limitations are scattered and not systematically addressed.

Presentation issues include typos (e.g., 'Broader Imapct'), undefined notation such as R_KL(s; C, Theta) in Theorem 1, dense tables, and some overstatements in the abstract/introduction (e.g., 'generalizes across five model sizes over ten watermarking schemes').

No code release is mentioned, and the method is sensitive to several weights (w1', w2, w3). Combined with per-scheme hyperparameter tuning, this limits practical reproducibility and external validation.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the attack is evaluated across five model scales (0.6B–8B), ten watermarking schemes spanning logit- and sampling-based families, four datasets, and two text lengths (500/1500 tokens), with ablations on training size, mixed keys, mixed watermarks, and OOD generators. This is a substantial and systematic robustness evaluation.

Demonstrates a practically important and well-supported finding: a detector-free, RL-based attacker trained on only ~100 short samples can substantially raise evasion success over prompting baselines (e.g., 93.3% vs 54.3% ESR on 500-token EWD for Qwen3-4B), establishing that current watermarking is far more fragile under adaptive attacks than average-case evaluations suggest.

The RL objective is well-motivated and reasonably engineered, combining a reparameterized semantic (P-SP) reward, a token-wise KL reward that pushes Q away from an approximated watermark distribution and toward a human-like distribution, and a perplexity penalty, with per-scheme weight configurations reported (Table 6).

The theoretical component is mathematically sound: the Donsker–Varadhan/sub-Gaussian derivation of the lower bound ρ* (Theorem 4.3, Appendix B) is correct, and the sub-Gaussianity of the normalized detector z-score (Proposition B.3) is proved under mild conditions; the D.9 correlation study (Pearson −0.77 to −0.90, Spearman ≤ −0.90) offers some empirical support that ρ* tracks removability.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: hyperparameters for all watermarkers (MarkLLM defaults), training details, learning rates, hardware, and per-scheme weights are provided, and code is claimed to be released.

The impact statement and dual-use discussion are appropriate for an attack paper, and the manuscript includes honest sensitivity analyses (proxy choice D.10, cross-watermark transferability D.14) that expose limitations.
weaknesses: Theory–method disconnect: the actual attack maximizes a heuristic objective D_KL(Q||P_wm) − D_KL(Q||P_h), which is not derived from or shown to minimize the KL adaptive radius. The theorem only gives a lower bound on robustness, and the central theoretical claim that optimizing context/parameters 'significantly reduces the approximated radius' is validated only by a post-hoc correlation table (D.9), not by computing ρ* for the attack.

The certificate ρ* relies on a very loose sub-Gaussian proxy (n²/(4V), which is Θ(n) even under perfect dependence per Proposition B.3/Remark B.5), so the bound is likely far from tight; the paper does not discuss tightness or whether the resulting radius is informative in practice.

Overstated headline: the abstract's 98.5% is the single best cell (1500-token Unigram, Qwen2.5-3B). The same model yields only 78.5% on 500-token Unigram and 58% on 1500-token KGW, and many other schemes are in the 60–85% range, so the abstract presents an unrepresentative best case as the general result.

Unexplained and counterintuitive length scaling: for Unigram the 1500-token ESR exceeds the 500-token ESR (98.5 vs 78.5 for Qwen2.5-3B; 90.2 vs 67.0 for Qwen3-0.6B), contradicting both intuition and the paper's narrative that long-form text is the hard regime.

Semantic-fidelity gap understates the trade-off: RLCracker's P-SP is systematically lower than baselines on long text (≈0.72–0.80 vs 0.80–0.86), and the ESR metric is defined with a P-SP > 0.7 cutoff, so part of the reported 'success' is achieved by sitting near that threshold. The claim of 'minimal semantic shift' is not well supported for the 1500-token setting.

Sensitivity to the P_wm proxy undermines reproducibility/robustness: replacing the 0.6B proxy with an 8B proxy drops EWD ESR from 91.5 to 57.0 and SWEET from 92.5 to 56.8 (Table 13), showing results depend heavily on an unconstrained design choice.

No error bars or confidence intervals are reported for the main results despite modest sample sizes (100–400 per setting), and per-scheme weight tuning is described as highly sensitive (Figure 5), raising concerns about variance and selection.

The 'generalizable' claim is partially undercut: a model trained on EWD transfers poorly to other watermark families (Table 20: 36.75% on PF vs 63.0% base), and the mixed-watermark remedy requires knowing the mixture in advance.

Presentation defects: the training objective in Section 4.2 of the main text is rendered garbled/repeated ('w_2\Delta w_3ppl(\pi_\theta, ...' repeated many times), which obscures the core algorithm; the clean version appears only in Appendix C.3.

Baseline comparison via the coupled ESR metric disadvantages methods that trade semantics for removal (e.g., SIRA's high Rem. but low P-SP yields near-zero ESR); a decoupled presentation would be fairer and more informative.

strengths: Broad empirical scope: the attack is evaluated across five model scales, ten watermarking schemes (logit- and sampling-based), multiple datasets, and several baselines (Base, Think, SysP, SIRA, DIPPER, GPT-4o), with detailed appendix tables (ESR, removal rate, P-SP, PPL, GPT-judge) that provide a reasonably complete picture.

The empirical findings on system prompts (SysP) and reasoning depth (Think, test-time scaling) as adversarial factors are genuinely useful and practically relevant to watermark robustness evaluation, and are supported by consistent trends across schemes and models.

The paper examines realistic conditions beyond the headline result: mixed-hash-key training, OOD watermarked text, data-efficiency ablations (50/100/200 samples), and cross-model generation, which strengthens the empirical narrative.
The impact statement responsibly acknowledges dual-use risks of watermark-removal tooling and suggests access controls and constructive diagnostic uses.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical contribution does not support its claims. The 'adaptive robustness radius' is explicitly a relaxed, distribution-level quantity, not the instance-level robustness it is framed against, so it does not 'certify' watermark robustness. The certificate ρ* depends on μ and σ², which are functions of the secret key and detector and are admitted to be inaccessible; the sub-Gaussian assumption (Appendix B.1) is trivially satisfied by any bounded score (Hoeffding), yielding a variance proxy n²/(4V) that grows with sequence length and is essentially vacuous. The theorem therefore reduces to a restatement of Donsker-Varadhan with no substantive content about watermark security.

The link between the theory and the algorithm is motivational rather than rigorous. The theory prescribes maximizing KL(Q||P_{X,c,θ}) for a fixed local watermark distribution, whereas RLCracker optimizes KL(Q||P_wm) − KL(Q||P_h) using ad-hoc proxy distributions (P_wm from paraphrasing watermarked text, P_h from the question), which are not the P of the theorem. The theoretical justification is therefore not actually instantiated by the method.

The generalization claim is overstated. The method trains a dedicated policy per watermark scheme with per-scheme weights (Table 6), and the cross-watermark transfer experiment (Appendix D.14) shows catastrophic failure (e.g., EWD-trained model drops to 13.3% on Unigram vs. 93.3% on EWD). This contradicts the framing of 'generalizing across ten watermarking schemes' and implies the attacker must know which watermark is present, weakening the black-box/'zero detector access' framing.

The headline comparison is not apples-to-apples: RLCracker is evaluated with the SysP prompt while GPT-4o and the other baselines are evaluated under Base prompts (noted in the text and tables), which inflates the reported gap (e.g., the 98.5% vs 6.75% contrast).

The proxy distributions are ad hoc and highly sensitive: Appendix D.10 shows EWD ESR collapsing from 91.5 to 57.0 when a stronger proxy generator is used, undermining robustness of the method and raising questions about the reliability of the reported numbers.

Presentation is poor and, in places, broken. The central training objective in Section 4.2 is garbled (repeated 'w_3 ppl(π_θ, ...' fragments), the section heading reads 'RLTracker' instead of 'RLCracker', and 'paraphraseer' typos recur. The main-text equation for the objective is effectively unreadable, which impedes reproducibility of the core method.

The theoretical metric is validated only by a correlation table over a handful of points per scheme (Appendix D.9), which is weak evidence for a claim that ρ* 'strongly tracks' removability, and the metric is not used anywhere in the actual attack pipeline.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating worst-case robustness of LLM watermarks under adaptive, high-capacity attacks rather than average-case paraphrasing.
Introduces the KL adaptive radius, a novel distributional certificate inspired by certified robustness and distributionally robust optimization, giving a principled lens on watermark vulnerability.
Proposes RLCracker, a practical RL-based black-box attack that requires only 100 watermarked samples, zero detector access, and remains effective on long-form text where many baselines fail.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five model scales, ten watermarking schemes, multiple token lengths, OOD data, mixed keys, mixed watermarks, and robust/semantic watermarks, with comparisons to SIRA, DIPPER, GPT-4o, DPO, and WS.
Reproducibility is strong: code is released, and the appendix provides detailed hyperparameters, prompts, watermark settings, and training configurations.
The impact statement responsibly acknowledges potential misuse and recommends access controls for attack implementations.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overstated. The adaptive robustness radius r* is intractable and not computed; the KL adaptive radius is a relaxation. Theorem 4.3 only lower-bounds r_KL via rho*, yet the paper claims optimizing context/model parameters can minimize the radius. Appendix B's argument that rho*=0 implies R_KL=0 is logically invalid: a zero lower bound does not imply a zero radius.

The attack objective is not rigorously derived from the theorem. RLCracker maximizes a heuristic token-wise KL difference, while P_wm and P_h are approximated by passing watermarked text or the original question through a reference model, not by the true local watermark distribution or human distribution.

The sub-Gaussian assumption is weakly justified. Proposition B.3 gives a variance proxy n^2/(4V) that grows with sequence length for long texts, making the certified radius very loose and potentially trivial. The assumption is also not verified for sampling-based schemes such as SynthID-Text and PF-Watermark.

The RL training is sensitive to reward weights, and the paper uses different weight configurations per watermarking scheme, raising concerns about tuning on evaluation performance. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the KL reward versus the semantic reward and perplexity penalty.

Evaluation concerns: the ESR threshold P-SP > 0.7 is relatively lenient, and long-text P-SP scores are sometimes around 0.72, so the claim of 'minimal semantic shift' is stronger than the evidence supports. The abstract highlights the best-case 98.5% Unigram result while many other settings are substantially lower.

Generalization is limited when the watermark family is unknown: cross-watermark transfer is poor (Table 20), and although mixed-watermark training helps, it still requires some examples from each target family. The attack also trains a dedicated model per watermark scheme in the main experiments.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not deeply discuss theoretical limitations, attack failure modes, or defense implications beyond a brief impact statement.
